reviewGate: Maintainer scholarly review required before these construct boundaries, rivals, or predictions are treated as accepted theory.

neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Self-sacralization requires the order to treat its own survival as sacred, not merely lawful or useful.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can attach devotion and obligation to the political community.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Patriotism can remain bounded and corrigible; self-sacralization makes the order's preservation morally non-negotiable.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can ask people to contribute labor, risk, or obedience.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Sacrificial demand requires surrendered goods to be framed as meaningful or necessary for the sacred order, not merely administratively requested.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both can compel suffering, killing, or dying.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Coercion describes compulsion; sacrificial demand codes the symbolic meaning and moral demand attached to surrendered human goods.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both evaluate whether sacrifice can be justified.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Sacrifice health scores whether sacrifice preserves personhood, truth, correction, and flourishing; it does not resolve all normative legitimacy questions.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both attend to the burden imposed by collective action.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Sacrifice health includes symbolic pathology and corrigibility, not only instrumental proportionality.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both restrain what authorities may demand.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Boundedness covers legal, moral, temporal, and symbolic limits on sacrifice, not only formal constitutional constraint.

neighboringConcepts.overlap: Both may justify constrained sacrifice during crisis.
neighboringConcepts.discriminantBoundary: Military necessity is a situational claim; sacrifice boundedness asks whether demands remain limited and corrigible.

scopeConditions: The political order faces or narrates an existential threat.
Sacrificial demands can be linked to preservation of the order rather than unrelated coercion.
rivalHypotheses: Sacrificial demand is explained by ordinary resource mobilization.
Sacrifice is explained by coercive capacity alone.
Threat perception increases sacrifice without any sacred self-preservation claim.
expectedObservations: Rhetoric or institutions link individual loss to the survival of the order.
Unbounded or pathological sacrifices become more likely where correction channels are blocked.
counterObservations: High sacrifice appears with no sacred survival claim.
Self-sacralizing orders repeatedly maintain bounded sacrifice under comparable threat without correction mechanisms.
discriminatingPredictions: Sacrificial demand should rise most sharply when threat language and sacred-order survival language coincide.
Bounded anti-sacrificial cases should show threat recognition without moral absolutization of the order's survival.
